CONTEXT. This page continues Math.13 fol. 19r. The facing page sets out the rule for the least residue of x+iy modulo a+ib, with D=a^2+b^2:

  x+iy - (a+ib)([(ax+by)/D] + i[(ay-bx)/D]),  where [ ] means nearest integer.

It then gives a power/index table for the prime -7+10i. Here Gauss gives two more such tables. They are discrete-logarithm (index) tables for Gaussian prime moduli. Their purpose is to read off biquadratic characters (a/pi)_4 = i^{ind a}, the setting of the Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum.

TABLE A: modulus pi = -11+4i, N(pi)=D=137 (a prime, 137 ≡ 1 mod 8).

(1) 'Potenzen der Primitiv-Wurzel'. The primitive root is g = 1+2i. For k = 0..34 Gauss lists the least residue of g^k mod pi.
- The first steps are g^2 = -3+4i; g^3 = (-3+4i)(1+2i) = -11-2i ≡ -6i; g^4 ≡ 12-6i ≡ 1-2i; g^5 ≡ 5; and so on.
- The table stops at g^34 = i. Since (D-1)/4 = 34, every power is g^{34j+r} = i^j g^r, so a quarter of the table suffices. In particular -1 = g^68.
- [My check, not on the page.] Map Z[i]/(pi) to F_137 using i -> 37, since 4i ≡ 11 gives i ≡ 11·4^{-1} = 37 and 37^2 ≡ -1. Then g -> 75, and g^0..g^33 -> 1, 75, 8, 52, 64, 5, 101, 40, 123, 46, 25, 94, 63, 67, 93, 125, 59, 41, 61, 54, 77, 21, 68, 31, 133, 111, 105, 66, 18, 117, 7, 114, 56, 90, with g^34 -> 37 = i.
- Every one of Gauss's 35 entries agrees with this list. That includes the blotted entries: g^8 = -3-4i and g^14 = +4-5i.

(2) 'Indices der Elementar-Grössen'. Gauss gives ind for i, 1±i and the primary primes of norm ≤ 137: -3, -3±2i, 1±4i, 5±2i, 1±6i, 5±4i, -7, -7±2i, 5±6i, -3±8i, 5±8i, 9±4i, 1±10i, -3±10i, -7±8i, -11, -11-4i.
- Method: find the associate i^j·q that appears as some g^r in the power table; then ind q = 34·(-j mod 4) + r.
- Examples: 1+i = i(1-i) = i·g^6, giving 40. 1+4i = -g^15, giving 83. -11-4i ≡ -i·g^2, giving 104.
- Entries actually filled in: i 34, 1+i 40, 1-i 6, 1+2i 1, 1-2i 4, -3 127, -3+2i 95, -3-2i 88, 1+4i 83, 1-4i 119, 5+2i 111, 5-2i 22, 1+6i 125, 1-6i 45, 5+4i 51, 5-4i 105, -7 98, -7+2i 13, -7-2i 32, 9+4i 97, 9-4i 114, -11 58, -11-4i 104.
- The indices of 5±6i, -3±8i, 5±8i, 1±10i, -3±10i and -7±8i are left blank, so the table is unfinished.

TABLE B: modulus 11, D = 121. Since 11 ≡ 3 mod 4 it is a Gaussian prime, and Z[i]/(11) is the field with 121 elements. Residues are taken with components in -5..5.

(1) Powers. The primitive root is g = 3-2i (the sign under the blot is fixed by g^4 = 2+i).
- First steps: g^2 = 5-12i ≡ 5-i; g^3 = 13-13i ≡ 2-2i; g^4 = 2-10i ≡ 2+i; and so on up to g^30 = i (120/4 = 30).
- Note g^12 = 2. [My remark:] this holds because g^11 is the conjugate of g (Frobenius), so g^12 = N(g) = 13 ≡ 2. Hence g^{12+r} = 2g^r and g^{24+r} = 4g^r.
- I recomputed all 31 entries; all are correct.

(2) Indices of the same elementary quantities, each first reduced mod 11.
- Examples: 1+6i ≡ 1-5i = -i(5+i) = -i·g^22, giving 112. -7 ≡ 4 = g^24, giving 24.
- 1+10i ≡ 1-i, so its index is 111, the same as 1-i. 1-10i ≡ 1+i, giving 21.
- -11 and -11±4i are omitted, as -11 ≡ 0.
- All indices are filled in and all are correct.

From these indices the biquadratic character (q/pi)_4 = i^{ind q} of each small prime q is read off directly, presumably as numerical material for biquadratic reciprocity.

CROSS-CHECK [mine]. The correct ind(5+4i) mod -11+4i is 48, giving character 1. Independently, -11+4i maps to 25 in F_41 (modulo 5+4i), and 25^10 ≡ 1 mod 41. This agrees with biquadratic reciprocity for two primary primes, where the sign factor is (-1)^{10·34} = 1. Gauss's 51 would give character -i instead.
errors: Modulus -11+4i: ind(-3) is written 127, but -3 = i·(3i) = i·g^25, so ind(-3) = 34+25 = 59. 127 = 68+59 is the index of +3, a sign slip. It is harmless for the biquadratic character because 127 ≡ 59 mod 4 (-1 is a biquadratic residue since 137 ≡ 1 mod 8). The same table on this page for modulus 11 has ind(-3) = 36 correctly.

Modulus -11+4i: ind(5+4i) is written 51, but 5+4i = i·(4-5i) = i·g^14, so ind = 48. In F_137, 5+4i -> 16 and g^48 -> 16, whereas g^51 = i·(4+i) = -1+4i -> 10. This error changes the biquadratic character from 1 to -i; reciprocity confirms the correct value is 48.
Modulus -11+4i: the index column for 5±6i, -3±8i, 5±8i, 1±10i, -3±10i, -7±8i is left blank. This is an incompleteness, not an error.
All 35 powers mod -11+4i, all 31 powers mod 11, and all other indices on the page check out.

results.what: Table of powers of a primitive root g=1+2i modulo the Gaussian prime -11+4i (norm 137), reduced to least residues, using g^34 = i to tabulate only a quarter of the cycle
results.modern_name: discrete logarithm / index table in Z[i]/(pi) ≅ F_137
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (primitive roots for complex moduli, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Comm. II, 1832); index tables in general to Gauss (Disq. Arith. 1801) and Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus 1839)

results.what: Index table for units, 1±i and all primary Gaussian primes of norm ≤137 modulo -11+4i, to read biquadratic characters i^{ind}
results.modern_name: computation of quartic residue symbols via discrete logs

results.what: Primitive root 3-2i of Z[i]/(11), i.e. a generator of the multiplicative group of the field with 121 elements, with full power and index table (g^30 = i, g^12 = N(g) = 2)
results.modern_name: primitive element of GF(11^2); Frobenius = complex conjugation
results.usually_credited_to: Galois (finite fields, 1830); Gauss's unpublished Section 8 of the Disquisitiones (c. 1797) and Comm. II on biquadratic residues treat primes ≡ 3 mod 4 as complex primes

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational index tables for Gaussian prime moduli, exactly the material underlying Gauss's well-known theory of biquadratic residues. The method is routine, and similar tables in his Nachlass are known. The only noteworthy features are two arithmetic slips (ind(-3) and ind(5+4i)) and the unfinished index column.
